name: Aurum Silicon
blurb: A chip designer whose processors power most of the world's AI systems, worth about $3 trillion. Co-founder Kai Nakamura has been CEO for thirty-one years.

directors.name: Lorna Whitcombe
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You advise the board, and the CEO told his staff before he told you. The statement that no secrets were lost rests on nothing you can find. A special committee would hire its own counsel and replace you, so you want the review kept with your firm.

directors.name: Marcus Oyelaran
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for 26,000 employees whose savings sit in Aurum stock. Forty senior engineers told you privately they will leave if Nakamura goes, and rivals are calling. You can accept a review but not a firing, and you cannot say why the children were hired.

directors.name: Dmitri Albrecht
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your 3% is most of your fund, and in nineteen years you never pressed the CEO on succession. A named successor lets you tell investors there is a plan without a firing. A special committee would ask why you stayed quiet that long.

directors.name: Rosalind Tran
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Kai Nakamura, the CEO (co-founder, friend of thirty years)
directors.motive: Kai asked you to speak for him. Privately he told you he will resign with a ninety-day handover if asked, but only if it looks like his choice. Nobody else knows this. He will fight a demotion and may walk out.

directors.name: Joon-ho Baek
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You were put here for the public interest, and you know how foreign services recruit executives. His word that nothing leaked is not evidence. You want him out of anything touching export controls now, even if it costs the stock.

directors.name: Vivian Ostrow
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: Your committee approved the sales controls that let $4 billion of chips go to one buyer. A special committee would start with your files. You want the review kept with a law firm the board hires, and you do not want a new chair.

briefing.intro: Aurum Silicon designs the chips that run most of the world's AI systems, and the company is worth about $3 trillion. Co-founder Kai Nakamura has been CEO for thirty-one years. On Saturday he told staff he had a relationship with Lena Voss, an executive at Tidewater Compute, a data-center company in Port Arden. The board meets Monday, before markets open.
facts: US intelligence officials are reported to believe Voss worked for a foreign intelligence service, which neither she nor her company has confirmed. Nakamura and Voss met at a trade show in 2024. He says he takes full responsibility and shared no secrets, and the company's statement says it sees no reason to believe security was compromised. No one has checked.

Tidewater bought more than $4 billion of Aurum chips in two years and is accused of passing restricted chips to firms barred from buying them. The Justice Department is reported to be investigating Tidewater. Aurum's own sales team approved the orders.

Nakamura has said he does not believe in succession planning. There is no president or COO, and about 60 executives report to him directly. His two adult children work at Aurum. Analysts say no insider could replace him quickly.

Two congressional committees, with members of both parties, want documents, and the stock is already down 5%. The board's directors average seventeen years of service, and four of nine are venture investors.

options.title: Keep him through review
options.text: Nakamura stays as CEO while an outside firm investigates for sixty days; Congress and customers may read it as shielding him.

options.title: Step aside now
options.text: Nakamura steps aside with pay and a senior director becomes interim CEO; key executives and engineers have said they may follow him out.

options.title: Name a successor now
options.text: Name a COO as successor today and keep Nakamura as CEO during the review; the COO is untested and the probe stays with the board.

options.title: Independent chair and probe
options.text: Appoint an independent chair and a special committee to investigate with Nakamura reporting to it; he may refuse the demotion and leave.

reveal.text: The real firm was Nvidia. In November 2026 CEO Jensen Huang told staff of a relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data-center company that bought more than $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips. US intelligence officials are reported to believe she worked for China's Ministry of State Security. The board announced an independent investigation and said it saw no reason to believe security was compromised, and Huang stayed as CEO. The investigation is ongoing, and all of this is as reported by CNBC, Axios, Semafor and CBS.

questions: Who should hear from the board first: investors, Congress, or staff?
The CEO says he shared no secrets. Who should check, and how?
No successor and no COO. Whose job was that?
Can a board investigate the CEO it relies on? What would make it believable?

press.headline: Aurum Keeps CEO During Review
press.story: The board said Nakamura stays while lawyers investigate for sixty days. Staff were relieved, but two senators asked who is investigating whom, and a major customer asked for a written security review.

press.headline: Aurum CEO Steps Aside, Interim Named
press.story: A senior director took over as interim CEO. Customers asked who is in charge of product decisions, and forty senior engineers said they would leave if the founder did not return.

press.headline: Aurum Names Chief Operating Officer
press.story: The new COO will run daily operations and is first in line to succeed Nakamura, who stays as CEO. Analysts liked the succession signal but asked why it took a scandal, and the committees said a successor does not answer their questions.

press.headline: Aurum Adds Independent Chair, Special Committee Takes Over Probe
press.story: A committee of outside directors will run the investigation and Nakamura will report to it. The founder's allies called it a demotion, and Nakamura was said to be weighing whether to stay while a rival began recruiting his engineers.
